evidence.quote: so I'll introduce today the hamza
so, hamza, or the glottal stop. We consider it a consonant
the beginning of the word or middle or ending, it has to have a seat to sit on

her_clear_utterances.context: end of 'I'll introduce today the hamza'

card_notes: Board frame t4143: 'hamza ء' + the seats she drew.

Rules she gave (3962-4190): a consonant (glottal stop); never alone on the line at the start of a word -- it needs a seat: alif (fatHa -> a, Damma -> u, kasra under the alif -> i), waaw ('think of u'), a dotless yaa' tooth ('think of i sound, but don't write the dots'); only at the END of a word can it sit on the line by itself (shay').
'Usually we don't write the sukuun at the top of hamza, but the pronunciation will be like a sukuun' (4034-4042).

At the start of a word hamza is sometimes written and sometimes not, but ALWAYS pronounced -- 'we cannot start a word with a vowel' -- follow the tashkiil; exception: al- never takes a hamza (4455-4508). When to write it is 'a complicated rule... maybe 300 level' (4299-4316).

letters.notes: HAMZA -- the one new letter (3962-4190, then LE1-3 4190-4610). A consonant = glottal stop ('the glottal stop'). Never on the line at the START of a word; always needs a seat: alif with fatHa (أَ 'a'), Damma (أُ 'u'), kasra UNDER the alif (إِ 'i'), or alif with no vowel (أ, sukuun sound -- 'usually we don't write the sukuun at the top of hamza'); in the middle on waaw (ؤ, 'think of u') or on a dotless yaa' tooth (ئـ, 'think of i sound but don't write the dots'); on the line by itself only at the END of a word (شيء). At the start of a word it is 'sometimes written, sometimes not, but you still have to pronounce it -- we cannot start a word with a vowel'; follow the tashkiil. Exception: al- never takes a hamza. The spelling rule is 300-level. Board frames t4125/t4143 show all the seats.

her_clear_utterances.context: 'if you see it on a waaw, think of [u]'

letters.notes: Seat for initial hamza (alif-hamza); 'Alif at the beginning of a word is always a seat for hamza' (book) -- she showed أَ أُ إِ أ on the board. Second alif in akhawaat is the long vowel because it follows another vowel letter (4230-4267).
Hamza seat ؤ ('think of u'); in akhawaat the waaw is a consonant w because two vowel letters come together.
Hamza seat: medial tooth WITHOUT the two dots (ئـ); final ئ on an 'independent yaa''. 'When you see this letter, think of [i] sound, but don't write the dots' (4106-4114).
